title: 101 Travis Config for Deployment

segments.text: Now that our elastic bean stock instance has been created, we're going to start to configure
Travis CI to automatically deploy our application over to AWS once our test has successfully
passed.
So to do so, we're going to add some more configuration to the Travis.eml file that we had created
inside of our root project directory.
I'm going to open up my code editor and then inside of here, I'm going to find the Travis.eml
file.
We'll recall that we currently have the before install and script sections inside of here.
And both of those are concerned solely with putting together our initial image and then
running some tests using that image.
I'm going to add in another section towards the bottom of this file called as you might
guess deploy.
So inside this section, we're going to add in a bunch of configuration to tell Travis CI exactly
how to take our application and deploy it off to AWS.
Now, some of these settings that we're going to put in here are going to be a little bit
laborious.
So I really got to ask you to watch really closely and make sure that you follow along
as closely as possible.
Now, the first option we're going to add in here is going to be really easy and straightforward.
We're going to say provider is elastic, bean stock, all one word like so.
Travis CI comes pre-configured to deploy our application to a handful of different providers
or hosting providers such as AWS or Digital Ocean or whichever other you can possibly
imagine.
And so by just saying provider, elastic, bean stock, we're essentially telling Travis CI
that, hey, we want you to use this set of instructions to attempt to automatically deploy
our application.
So by just specifying that right there, Travis CI is going to really do a lot of stuff
for us automatically.
Now, we're going to still provide a lot of other options in here as well to just provide
some further customization.
The next one we're going to provide is region.
Now, region is going to be a little bit of a tough one because the region that you're
going to specify depends upon exactly where you originally created your elastic, bean stock
instance.
Let me tell you what I mean by that.
If you flip back over to your elastic, bean stock dashboard, which you look like this,
I want you to look very closely at that URL again.
I'm going to copy the URL and I'm going to put it over into my code editor just so you can
read mine very easily.
So when you created your elastic, bean stock instance, you created it in a particular
region.
And when I say region, I'm talking about like area of the earth or kind of continent,
essentially.
So me personally, I created the region in the, to me, the elastic bean stock instance
in the region, US West to right here, you need to specify whatever region you were
elastic, bean stock instance was just created in.
You might have something like US East one, US West one, you might have a totally different
country inside of here.
It's going to be up to you to find whichever code it is and you're going to take that
code and put it in as the region wrapped inside of quotes.
So I'll say US, dash west, dash two.
And again, what you put in here is going to be whatever you see right there, but for the
elastic, bean stock.com.
All right.
So once we got that in there, we're then going to add in a couple other options.
We're going to specify the name of our app.
Now the name of the app is the same name that you had created back over here on the
elastic, bean stock dashboard.
So you see how we have all applications right here?
The first word right after that is the name of your app.
So I called my Docker, you might have called you or something like Docker dash react.
Whatever you have right there, you're going to take it, letter for letter, and you're
going to enter it in as the app right here.
And so for me, I'm going to put in simply Docker like so.
The next configuration piece we're going to add in is the environment name.
So when we created the application of Docker or Docker react, that's kind of just setting
up a common set of configuration.
The actual app that's running inside of here, it's not really referred to as an app,
but instead is referred to as an environment.
And so the environment is going to be the last piece on there.
For me, my environment name is Docker-m.
So you're going to take whatever is listed right there.
You're going to copy it and then we're going to put it right in there for ENV.
All right.
So that's looking pretty good.
Now the next piece of configuration here is going to be just a little bit nastier
than the two we just went through.
We're going to put in a bucket name.
So when Travis decides to deploy your code base, it's going to take all of the files
inside of your GitHub repository.
It's going to zip them all up into one single file, and then it's going to copy all
them over to an S3 bucket, which is essentially a hard drive running on AWS.
Once it copies all those files over, Travis si's then going to essentially poke at
Elastic Beanstalk and say, hey, I just uploaded this new zip file.
Use that to redeploy your application.
So we need to provide the name of the bucket that Travis si is going to put our zip
file into.
Now, that might sound like it's a little complicated.
The good news here is that this has been a S3 bucket that is already automatically generated
for you when you initially created the Elastic Beanstalk instance.
All we have to do is get the name of it.
So to get the name, we're going to go up to services up here, and then we're going to do
a search for S3.
And then you should see S3 scalable storage in the cloud.
Then on here, you're going to look up and down this list.
You'll notice that I have a tremendous number, but hopefully you'll have a little bit
fewer than what I have.
You're looking for something like this right here.
You should see one called Elastic Beanstalk, dash, and then the name of the region that
your bucket or something that your Elastic Beanstalk was placed in.
So like I just said, mine is US-2, so I'm going to be looking for something like Elastic
Beanstalk, dash, US-2, and mine is right there.
So I'm going to look on that thing, and then I'll see the name of the bucket right up
here.
Now, I have enough time to select it myself.
There we go.
If I just right click it, I get the full selection and I can copy it.
So I'll take that back over, and for the bucket name, I'm going to paste it in like
so.
And then we're going to also do the bucket path.
So this bucket right here, or this S3 bucket that's holding all these different files,
it gets reused for all of the different Elastic Beanstalk environments that you create.
So as you can see, I've got a couple of different environments that have been created over
time.
And so inside of here, I'm going to be looking for the folder that is essentially
the name of my project.
Now when you first create your Elastic Beanstalk instance, chances are it's not going
to create a folder by default automatically.
That folder is only going to be created the first time that you do a deploy.
So by default, the bucket path that you're supposed to use is going to be exactly equal
to the app name.
So you see, I have app right here, I'm going to use the exact name for my bucket path.
So for me, I have Docker as my app name, and I'm going to copy that right down to bucket
path.
And you might have used something like Docker React, so make sure if you have the different
app name, make sure you use it in there as well.
All right, so now last thing we're going to do in here for right now, remember back
to the entire deployment flow that we spoke about a while ago, we had said that we wanted
to make sure that any time we deploy or see me we push our code up to a feature branch on
their GitHub repository, we had said that we're going to make a pull request to merge
into master.
And we had said that the master branch was essentially going to be our very special
branch, anytime we merge code into master, that means it is time to deploy our application.
If we just merge code or push code up to the feature branch, we don't want to deploy
the app, we don't want to deploy the app using just the feature branch.
The feature branch is for active development and it might have new features that are not
ready to be deployed.
So last piece of configuration that we're going to put in there for right now, we're
going to say only attempt to deploy the application when the master branch gets some
new code.
So it's a very last thing that I'll do for right now, I'll say on branch master, like
so.
And so as you might guess, this essentially means any time we push code to branch
master, that's the time to deploy.
All right, so I think that's good for right now, now there's going to be two other
tiny pieces of configuration that we have to add in, but those are going to take just
a little bit of time.
So take a quick pause right here and continue the next section and handle those two
last pieces.
